passages.happening:
“To the angel of the church in Sardis write: These are the words of the One who holds the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars. I know your deeds; you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead. Wake up and strengthen what remains, which was about to die; for I have found your deeds incomplete in the sight of My God” (verses 1-2).

“Remember, then, what you have received and heard. Keep it and repent. If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know the hour when I will come upon you. But you do have a few people in Sardis who have not soiled their garments, and because they are worthy, they will walk with Me in white” (verses 3-4).

“Like them, he who overcomes will be dressed in white. And I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life, but I will confess his name before My Father and His angels. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
Sardis had once been the capital of the kingdom of Lydia, whose king Croesus was famous for his wealth; the Lydians are credited with some of the first coins. Its citadel stood on a steep hill and was thought impossible to take. Yet it fell by surprise to the Persian king Cyrus around 546 BC, when soldiers climbed an unguarded slope, and again to the Seleucid king Antiochus III in 214 BC. In AD 17 a great earthquake wrecked the city, and the emperor Tiberius helped rebuild it.

Many commentators hear that history in Christ's words. ‘Wake up.’ ‘I will come like a thief.’ A city that trusted its walls and did not keep watch had been taken twice.

The church had ‘a reputation for being alive’. People spoke well of it. But Christ says, ‘you are dead’. He judges by what he sees, not by what others say. There is almost no praise here, only a call: wake up, strengthen what is left, remember what you received, keep it, and turn back.

Yet even in Sardis there were ‘a few people’ who had not soiled their clothes. In the ancient world white robes were worn at festivals and celebrations of victory. Christ promises that they will walk with him in white.

And he promises not to ‘blot out’ the name of the one who overcomes from ‘the Book of Life’. Cities kept lists of their citizens, from which a name could be struck. Christ's list is different. The one who overcomes is kept on it, and Christ will speak his name before the Father.
passages.ot:
The Book of Life is an old picture. Moses prayed, “please blot me out of the book that You have written” (Exodus 32:32). The psalm speaks of those who are “blotted out of the Book of Life” (Psalm 69:28). And Daniel promises rescue for “everyone whose name is found written in the book” (Daniel 12:1).

White clothing as a picture of being made right with God is Isaiah's: “for He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10).
passages.hard:
‘I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life.’ Does this mean a name can be blotted out? Should I be afraid that mine will be?

Christians read this promise in line with their wider views on whether a believer can fall away. Reformed teaching holds that those God has truly called and made his own will persevere to the end, because God keeps them. Arminian and Wesleyan teaching holds that a true believer can turn away from Christ in unbelief and be finally lost, and that the warnings of Scripture describe a real danger. Lutheran and Catholic teaching each hold that grace can be lost, and point the troubled to Christ. These notes do not choose. The doctrine study on assurance and perseverance sets the views out more fully.

Either way, the sentence is spoken as a promise to those who overcome, not as a threat to frightened believers.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether your faith, or your church, is living on a reputation. Ask what ‘wake up’ would mean for you this week. And ask what you received at first that you need to remember and keep.

passages.happening:
“To the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: These are the words of the One who is holy and true, who holds the key of David. What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open” (verse 7).

“I know your deeds. See, I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut. For you have only a little strength, yet you have kept My word and have not denied My name. Look at those who belong to the synagogue of Satan, who claim to be Jews but are liars instead. I will make them come and bow down at your feet, and they will know that I love you” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
Philadelphia was the youngest of the seven cities. It was founded in the second century BC by the kings of Pergamum and named for the brotherly love between King Attalus II and his brother. It suffered badly in the earthquake of AD 17 and in tremors after it. The geographer Strabo wrote that many of its people lived outside the city for fear of falling walls.

Christ comes as ‘the One who is holy and true, who holds the key of David’. In Isaiah, the key of David's house was given to a faithful steward, Eliakim, so that what he opened no one could shut. Christ holds that key now. He decides who comes into God's house.

And he has set before this church ‘an open door, which no one can shut’. Most read it as an opportunity for witness, or as entrance into his kingdom. The church has ‘only a little strength’. It is small and weak. But it has kept his word and not denied his name. Like Smyrna, it receives no rebuke.

Then Christ speaks of ‘the synagogue of Satan’, as he did to Smyrna. Here too there was conflict with some in the city's synagogue. Christ promises that they will come to know ‘that I love you’. The words echo promises God made to Israel in Isaiah. Here they assure a small, weak church that it is loved.
passages.ot:
The key of David is from Isaiah, where God gives it to Eliakim: “I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open” (Isaiah 22:22).

The promise that others would bow down echoes Isaiah's word to Zion: “The sons of your oppressors will come and bow down to you” (Isaiah 60:14). And God's love is Isaiah's too: “Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you” (Isaiah 43:4).
passages.hard:
What does ‘the synagogue of Satan’ mean here, at Philadelphia?

It means what it meant at Smyrna (2:9), and it must be read with the same care. It is not a statement about the Jewish people. John himself was a Jew, and his book is full of Israel's Scriptures. The phrase speaks of a local conflict in one city in the first century, among people who all claimed to be heirs of Israel's God. Some in the synagogue at Philadelphia were opposing the Christians there. Christ's charge, ‘who claim to be Jews but are liars instead’, is the language of a family quarrel about who is truly living as God's people, like Paul's “a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly” (Romans 2:29). It is not a verdict on a people.

Phrases like this were later torn from their setting and used by Christians to justify contempt and violence against Jews. That reading is false. This site rejects it, and the note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why. Nothing in this verse says anything about Jewish people as a whole, then or now. The promise in it is for a small, frightened church: ‘they will know that I love you’.
passages.asks: Ask what door Christ might be opening in front of you, even if you have only a little strength. Ask whether you have kept his word when it would have been easier to let it go. And ask whether you have ever heard this verse used against Jewish people, and how you would answer.

passages.t: Kept in the hour of testing
passages.happening:
“Because you have kept My command to persevere, I will also keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth. I am coming soon. Hold fast to what you have, so that no one will take your crown” (verses 10-11).

“The one who overcomes I will make a pillar in the temple of My God, and he will never again leave it. Upon him I will write the name of My God, and the name of the city of My God (the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from My God), and My new name. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
Notice the word play. ‘Because you have kept’ my word, ‘I will also keep you’. Those who kept faith are kept.

‘The hour of testing’ is coming on ‘the whole world’. Christians have read this in different ways (see below). But what the verse plainly offers this small church is Christ's own commitment: because they held on, he will hold them. ‘Hold fast to what you have, so that no one will take your crown.’

Then the promises, which fit Philadelphia closely. A city that had been shaken by earthquakes, whose people lived outside for fear of falling walls, is promised: the one who overcomes will be ‘a pillar in the temple of My God’, and ‘will never again leave it’. And a city that had taken new names in honour of emperors, Neocaesarea and later Flavia, is promised a better name: the name of God, the name of his city, and Christ's own new name.
passages.ot:
The city that bears God's name is Ezekiel's last word: “the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE” (Ezekiel 48:35).

And the new name is Isaiah's promise: “You will be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow” (Isaiah 62:2).
passages.hard:
‘I will also keep you from the hour of testing.’ Does this mean the church will be taken out of the world before a time of great trouble?

This verse is one of the key texts in the debate over the timing of the rapture, the gathering of believers to meet Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Christians read it in several ways, and these notes do not choose.

Pretribulationists, especially in dispensational premillennialism, read ‘keep you from the hour’ as a promise to remove the church from the time of trial itself, which they take to be a future seven-year tribulation. They note that the hour comes upon ‘the whole world’, not only Philadelphia.

Posttribulationists and many others read it as a promise of protection through the trial rather than removal from it. They point to Jesus' prayer in John 17:15, which uses the same verb and preposition: “I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one.”

Amillennial and preterist readers often see the hour of testing as a trial in the first century, or as the trials that come again and again through the whole age of the church.

Each view is held by faithful Christians. What the verse plainly gives a small, weak church is Christ's promise to keep them. Paul gives no date, John gives no date, and no one should set one. Nor should anyone claim that a nation, a war, a leader or any event of our own day is what this verse describes.
passages.asks: Ask what you are holding on to, and whether you trust Christ to hold you. Ask what it would mean to be ‘a pillar’ that never has to leave God's house. And ask whether you are more anxious about the timing of the end or about being faithful now.

passages.happening:
“To the angel of the church in Laodicea write: These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true Witness, the Originator of God’s creation. I know your deeds; you are neither cold nor hot. How I wish you were one or the other! So because you are lukewarm—neither hot nor cold—I am about to vomit you out of My mouth!” (verses 14-16).

“You say, ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.’ But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked. I counsel you to buy from Me gold refined by fire so that you may become rich, white garments so that you may be clothed and your shameful nakedness not exposed, and salve to anoint your eyes so that you may see. Those I love, I rebuke and discipline. Therefore be earnest and repent” (verses 17-19).
passages.hearers:
Laodicea lay in the Lycus valley, about a hundred miles east of Ephesus. It was a wealthy centre of banking, of a glossy black wool, and of medicine; a medical school was linked with the area, and an eye remedy called Phrygian powder was famous. After an earthquake in AD 60, the historian Tacitus records, Laodicea rebuilt from its own wealth without help from Rome. Paul's letter to the Colossians mentions the church there (Colossians 4:13-16).

Christ comes as ‘the Amen, the faithful and true Witness’. ‘Amen’ is a word used of God in Isaiah. He is the final guarantee of what is true. And he is ‘the Originator of God’s creation’, its source and ruler.

To this church he says no word of praise at all. ‘You are neither cold nor hot.’ Laodicea had no good water of its own. It brought water by aqueduct from springs several miles away, and by the time it arrived it was lukewarm and full of minerals. Nearby Hierapolis had hot springs used for healing, and Colossae had cold, fresh water. Many readers think Christ's words play on this: hot water heals, cold water refreshes, lukewarm water is good for nothing and makes you want to spit it out.

The church said, ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.’ Christ quotes its own words back to it. Then he answers each of the city's prides. Its banks: buy from me gold refined by fire. Its black wool: buy white garments. Its eye medicine: buy salve for your eyes, so you may see.

And then the turn. ‘Those I love, I rebuke and discipline.’ The sharpest message of the seven comes from love.
passages.ot:
‘The Amen’ is a word used of God in Isaiah: “whoever takes an oath in the land will swear by the God of truth” (Isaiah 65:16), where ‘truth’ is, in Hebrew, ‘amen’.

The boast ‘I am rich’ was Israel's too: “And Ephraim boasts: ‘How rich I have become! I have found wealth for myself’” (Hosea 12:8).

And loving discipline is the proverb's: “for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:12).
passages.hard:
What does ‘neither cold nor hot’ mean? Is it better to be cold toward God than lukewarm?

Readers take it in two main ways. Many, noting Laodicea's piped water, think ‘hot’ and ‘cold’ are both good: hot water heals, as at Hierapolis, and cold water refreshes, as at Colossae. On this reading the problem is not a lack of feeling but uselessness. The church neither healed nor refreshed anyone. An older reading takes ‘hot’ as zeal for God and ‘cold’ as open rejection, so that even open hostility would be better than indifference. The water background is widely accepted, though not by everyone. These notes do not choose.

Either way, the cure is the same: see your real need, receive from Christ what only he can give, and turn back. And the rebuke comes, Christ says, from love.
passages.asks: Ask where you say, in effect, ‘I need nothing’. Ask whether your faith heals or refreshes anyone, or whether it has become lukewarm. And ask what Christ might be offering you, gold, white clothes or sight, that you think you already have.

passages.happening:
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me” (verse 20).

“To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne, just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (verses 21-22).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the most famous verses in the Bible, and it is worth seeing where it stands. Christ is speaking to the church at Laodicea, the lukewarm church that said it needed nothing. He is outside its door. The Lord of creation stands at the door of his own church and knocks.

Then the invitation narrows to one person: ‘If anyone hears My voice and opens the door’. Each member of the church can answer, even if the church as a whole does not. And what Christ offers is a meal together. In the ancient world, to eat with someone was to share friendship and fellowship.

Christians have long used this verse to invite people to come to Christ for the first time, and the words do speak to anyone who hears his voice. But its first setting is a church that had shut him out without noticing. It is a word to believers and churches as much as to those outside.

The last promise of the seven is the greatest: to sit with Christ on his throne, as he overcame and sat with his Father on his. The image of the door runs on into the next chapter, where John sees ‘a door standing open in heaven’ (4:1) and is shown the throne, and the Lamb who overcame by being slain.
passages.ot:
The lover knocking at the door is the Song's picture: “My beloved is knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister, my darling’” (Song of Solomon 5:2).

And sharing a table with God is the psalm's hope: “You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies” (Psalm 23:5).
passages.hard:
‘I stand at the door and knock.’ Is this verse about a person becoming a Christian, or about a church?

In its setting it is spoken to a church: the lukewarm church at Laodicea, which thought it needed nothing and had left Christ outside. That is its first meaning. It calls believers and churches who have grown comfortable to open the door to Christ again.

But the invitation is also personal: ‘If anyone hears My voice and opens the door’. Christ speaks to each one who hears. So Christians have also used the verse to invite people to come to him, and the words fit. The setting does not cancel that use; it deepens it. The same Christ who calls the outsider in also knocks on the doors of churches that have shut him out.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have left Christ outside some door in your life, or your church has. Ask what it would mean to hear his voice and open. And ask what it means to you that he wants to sit at your table.
